title: The Road from Madrid
subtitle: A Pilgrim's Guide to the Camino de Madrid
author: CaminoPlus
rights: © 2026 CaminoPlus. All rights reserved. Passages quoted from the classics are in the public domain and are credited where they appear.
ai_disclosure: Written with AI assistance (Claude, by Anthropic), under the direction of CaminoPlus. Facts in the guides are listed with their sources; routes, closures and services change, so check local information before you walk.

spans.t: The Camino de Madrid leaves the capital of Spain to the north, climbs the granite Sierra de Guadarrama by a Roman road, passes the Roman aqueduct of Segovia, crosses the pine woods and the cereal plains of Castile, and ends at Sahagún, where it meets the Camino Francés. The app's catalog gives it ~320 km. It is a young pilgrim road laid on very old tracks, and the Confraternity of St James, a charity in the United Kingdom, says very few pilgrims walk it.
The promise of this book is simple.

By the last page you will know whether a quiet road from the capital is your Camino, how its thirteen walking days fall, where the long stretches without a village are, and what to check before you leave home.
How to use it

If you are a month or more away, read the next four chapters in order: the Way in brief, whether it suits you, when to go, and what to do before you go. Then read the days, one chapter for each landscape (the sierra, the pine country, the plains), and the chapter on the choices this road offers.
If you are on the road tonight, go straight to your day. Each says what the walking is like and where to take care.
If you are only dreaming, start with "Is this Camino for you?" and finish with "The inner Way".
What this book is not

It is not a live map, a timetable or a booking service. It names no hostels, cafes or shops, and it gives no prices, opening hours or bed counts. They change, and a wrong one costs a tired person dearly. For those, use the CaminoPlus app and ask locally.
This book was written with AI assistance, from public sources, and its author has not walked the road. So it gives you sources instead of memories, and it says plainly when the sources disagree.

On this road they disagree about the length, the pass, the number of stages and more. Two guides do most of the work here: the printed guide of the Madrid association that marked the route, which this book calls the Association's guide, and the pilgrim guide of the Junta de Castilla y León, the regional government, which it calls the Junta's guide. It names them each time it leans on one. Every distance carries a tilde,
, because it is approximate. Where something depends on the season (snow on the pass, heat, mist, a hostel that is shut), it says
check before you go
, and means it.
A few words you will meet
Buen Camino
, "good Way", is what pilgrims and locals say as you pass. An
albergue
is a pilgrims' hostel. The
credencial
is your pilgrim's passport, a folded card that you carry and have stamped along the way. Each stamp is a
sello
. A
puerto
is a mountain pass. A
cañada
is a historic drove road for livestock. The
Compostela
is the certificate the Pilgrim's Office in Santiago gives to those who meet its rules, which the chapter on arriving sets out.
Carry what you need, drink before you are thirsty, and take your time over the long hill.
Buen Camino.
Where it goes

The Camino de Madrid starts in the old centre of the capital, at the church of Santiago y San Juan Bautista on the Plaza de Santiago, a short walk from the Royal Palace. The Comunidad de Madrid's tourism pages give that as the start. The present church dates from 1811 and replaced a medieval one. Near it are two streets called Conchas and Veneras, "shells" and "scallop shells", which the Madrid association's guide points out as a sign of how old the pilgrim habit is here.

From there the road runs north and then north-west, almost in a straight line, to Sahagún. The Confraternity of St James describes it that way: over the Sierra de Guadarrama, through Segovia and Coca, across the Duero, and over the Tierra de Campos by Medina de Rioseco. It crosses two regions, the Comunidad de Madrid and Castilla y León, and four provinces: Madrid, Segovia, Valladolid and León.
The Madrid association's guide describes the ground the road crosses in several areas. This book uses five of them, joining the short slope below the pass on the Segovian side to the sierra:

items.t: The foothills, ~50 km from Madrid to Mataelpino, rising from ~650 m to ~1,000 m.
The Sierra de Guadarrama, over the Puerto de la Fuenfría, the highest point of the whole road.
The Tierra de Pinares, ~100 km of pine woods and sandy farmland between Segovia and Puente Duero.
The Montes Torozos, ~50 km of open uplands from Simancas to Medina de Rioseco.
The Tierra de Campos, ~60 km of cereal plain to Sahagún.

spans.t: At Sahagún you cross the river Cea by the Puente de Cantos, and the Association's guide says that from there you are on the Camino Francés.
How long it is, and who says so
The app's catalog gives ~320 km. Published figures differ:

items.t: The Confraternity of St James and the Association's guide say ~321 km.
The Spanish Wikipedia article gives ~324 km in its infobox.
The Junta de Castilla y León gives ~325 km, of which ~242 km are in Castilla y León.

The Association's own website, on its page about itself ("Quiénes somos"), gives ~360 km for "the Camino de Madrid proper" and a pass of "almost 1,900 m", figures that its printed guide does not repeat. This book follows the guide.

spans.t: The Confraternity says the road takes about two weeks without rest days. This book's thirteen walking days add up to ~325 km on the Junta's figures.

To Santiago itself the Association's guide counts ~676 km from Madrid, and the Junta's figures come to ~690 km. The last ~355 to ~365 km are the Camino Francés from Sahagún, which has its own book in this series,
The French Way
A young road on old ground

As a waymarked pilgrim route this one is new. The Madrid association, the Asociación de Amigos de los Caminos de Santiago de Madrid, which this book calls the Association, says it was founded in 1987. It says that between 1993 and 1996 it researched and traced the road from Madrid by Segovia and Valladolid to Sahagún and marked it with yellow arrows, presented it in September 1996 at an international congress of Jacobean associations in Carrión de los Condes, and published a first guide in 1999, a Holy Year. The Junta's guide calls it the most modern of the traditional routes to Santiago. The Association is a members' association, not a public body, so this book says "the Association says" wherever it leans on it.

The ground, though, is old. The Association's guide puts ~35 km between Colmenar Viejo and Cercedilla on the line of Roman secondary roads, and ~150 km from Cercedilla to Simancas on the line of the Roman road that the Antonine Itinerary, a Roman register of roads and distances, shows between Titulcia, in what is now the Madrid region, and Septimancas, today Simancas. For centuries the stockmen of the Mesta, the old Castilian association of livestock owners, used the same line to move their flocks between the cool mountains of summer and the warm lands of the south in winter. And for almost five hundred years, until the railway linked Castile and Galicia in the middle of the twentieth century, Galician reapers walked these tracks to cut the grain of the two Castiles. The Association calls them the nearest ancestors of today's pilgrims on this road.
What it feels like

Terrain first. The Association says ~97 percent of the way is earth, with asphalt under three percent, much of it on quiet local roads. The Confraternity calls it almost entirely footpaths and cañadas, and says it is well waymarked with yellow arrows. The Comunidad de Madrid added granite markers and wooden posts between 2001 and 2004, the Association's guide says, and the Junta's guide says the whole road is marked with arrows and milestones.

Then the shape of the walk. A city start with ~11 km of streets. Three days along the foot of the sierra. One big climb. A long drop to Segovia, then flat, wide country where the horizon does most of the work. Villages are small and, in places, far apart: the Association counts a ~7.6 km average between settlements, and ~31 km with none over the sierra.
It is quiet, and you should expect to be mostly alone with it. That is part of the road's character, and part of what it asks of you.
How hard is it?
The app's catalog rates the Camino de Madrid 3 on its scale of 1 to 5, the same as the Camino Francés. It rates the Camino del Norte and the Camino Primitivo 4, and the Camino Inglés 2.

The Confraternity of St James is blunt about where the difficulty sits. Apart from the climb over the Sierra de Guadarrama, it says, the walking is flat and easy, with no hills of any significance, and it is hard to get lost. The climb itself it puts at ~650 m in ~8 km up to the Puerto de la Fuenfría.
So the slopes are not the test. The test is made of other things:

items.t: One stiff day over the pass, ~31 km long, with no village on it.
Several days of ~25 to ~30 km on open ground, with little shade.
Sand in the pine woods, which slows you.
Services that thin out: the app's route notes say lodging is sparse, and the Association's guide counts ~14 km as the average distance between places that host pilgrims.
Solitude. You may go a day without meeting another walker.

spans.t: The Junta's guide says the ideal average is ~25 to ~30 km a day, and it suggests starting with shorter days until your body is used to it. After the first week, it says, you will be ready for longer ones. That is sound advice here, because the road's longest gaps come early.
Who it suits

items.t: Walkers who want quiet.
The Confraternity says the road appeals to people looking for solitude and the wide horizons of the
meseta
, the high plain of central Spain, and that very few pilgrims walk it.
Anyone who lives in Madrid, or lands there.

The Association traced and marked the road so that pilgrims could leave from the door of their own home. Its guide says Madrid has been the Spanish region that sends most pilgrims to Santiago by the cathedral's counts, as of 2014. You can step out of a flat and be on the Way.
People with about two weeks.
The Confraternity says Madrid to Sahagún can be walked in two weeks, and calls it a pilgrimage that suits a busy person.
Walkers who have done a Camino before
and want one with more path and less road. The Confraternity says there is more path and less road here than on any other pilgrim route.
Walkers who like to plan.
Things are open and shut here in ways a busy road would not need you to know. You will check the day ahead more often.

spans.t: You do not have to walk it as a pilgrim in the religious sense. The Association says it marked the road in a pilgrim spirit, not as a simple hiking route, and adds that nobody minds if you begin as a walker: the road is long, it says, and generous.
Who should choose another road

items.t: If you want company and a bed you never have to check,
choose the Camino Francés. It is far busier and has more services. This book's sister volume,
The French Way
, covers it.
If you want to arrive in Santiago in two weeks.

This road ends at Sahagún, ~355 to ~365 km short of the cathedral. Two weeks on this road bring you to a small town in Tierra de Campos, not to Santiago. At the Junta's ~25 to ~30 km a day, the Camino Francés from there is another ~12 to ~15 days.
If long hot days with no shade worry you,
think hard about July and August, or walk in spring or autumn. The next chapter has the details.
If you cannot comfortably walk a ~30 km day,
plan every long stretch with a split. The chapter on choices shows where.
If you are walking for a Compostela from a short walk,
the chapter on arriving explains what the Pilgrim's Office asks.

spans.t: None of this is a medical opinion. If you have a health worry, ask a doctor before you decide, and test your boots and your pack on a long day at home.
The short version

Nothing in the walking is technical. The road asks you to be self-reliant: to carry water, to start early, to read the weather over the sierra, and to be content with your own company. If that sounds like what you want, it is a good road.
Patterns, not forecasts. Weather on a high plain and on a mountain pass can change your plan in an hour, so use this chapter to choose a season and the app and the local forecast to choose a day.
The short answer

The app's route notes give April to June and September to October as the best months. The Confraternity of St James agrees in spirit: the road is walkable all year, it says, but spring and autumn are best, though they may be wet. It describes July to early September as extremely hot, with long stretches that have absolutely no shade, and winter as severe, with short days. It adds that there is snow on the Sierra de Guadarrama until May.
Spring

Long days and moderate heat are the case for April to June. The catch is the sierra. The Confraternity says snow can lie on the Guadarrama into May, and the Madrid association's guide warns that when it snows the Puerto de la Fuenfría can be impassable. If you cross early in the season, check conditions on the pass the day before, and read the choices chapter for the alternatives. Rain is possible in spring, as the Confraternity notes. Tierra de Campos is cereal country, so you may find the fields green in spring and cut and pale by the end of June.
Summer

July to early September is the hard season. For a sense of scale, Wikipedia's climate table for Valladolid, 1991 to 2020, gives a mean daily maximum of ~31 °C and a mean daily minimum of ~14 °C in July. For Segovia, at ~1,000 m, its table (1988 to 2010) gives ~30 °C and ~15 °C. For Madrid it says July daytime highs are ~32 to ~34 °C, often higher. Means hide the hot days. The road is open, much of it is without shade, and some stretches run for hours between villages. The Madrid association's summer leaflet asks for sun cream and a hat.
If you walk in summer, start at first light, finish before the afternoon heat, and treat the day's water as part of the plan. The next chapters come back to this.
The pine woods have one more risk. The Confraternity says wild camping in the pine forests is not recommended, because of the risk of fire.
Autumn

September and October are the second good window. Days are shorter than in spring, and rain returns, according to the Confraternity. The heat of August eases. Check which hostels are still open as the season ends: the Association's 2021 leaflets advise asking, even in summer, which ones are open for the next stretch.
Winter

Short days, cold, and fog. Wikipedia gives Valladolid a January mean daily maximum of ~8 °C and a minimum of about 1 °C, and says that morning fog is very typical in winter. The Association's guide warns that fog can be intense and persistent both in the sierra and in Castile, and advises carrying a means of orientation, or using the nearest road with care. Snow on the pass can shut it. Many people would not choose these months for a first Camino. If you do, the Confraternity's advice is to avoid the sierra in snow or bad weather, since there are no farms, villages or facilities up there.
Daylight

A standard solar calculation for the latitudes of this road gives about 9 hours of daylight around the winter solstice, about 12 hours at the equinoxes, and about 15 hours around midsummer. In midwinter a ~31 km day leaves little spare light, so plan a split.
Rain
Wikipedia gives Valladolid ~430 mm of rain a year and Segovia ~470 mm. Rain does come in spring and autumn, so carry a waterproof.
Crowds
You may have the road mostly to yourself in any month. The Confraternity says the pressures from tourism are few, perhaps except in Madrid itself.
Check before you go

Snow on the Fuenfría, heat warnings, fire restrictions in the pine woods, and which hostels are open. These change from week to week. The CaminoPlus app and the Association's website are the places to look.
The credencial

The credencial is your pilgrim's passport. The Pilgrim's Office in Santiago says it has two practical purposes: access to the hostels of the Way, and certification when you ask for the Compostela. It says the credencial gives no rights of its own, and that it must be issued by a parish, a confraternity, a diocese, an association of friends of the Way, or another Christian institution connected with the pilgrimage.

In Madrid, the Association issues it in person at its office, and its credencial page says it also gives a short talk on the Way at the same visit. Hours and conditions change, so look at the Association's website first. Better to have it before you leave the city than to look for one on the road. The Comunidad de Madrid's tourism page adds that you can have it stamped in Tres Cantos, at the end of the first day.

Stamps are normally collected where you sleep, the Office says, but also in parish churches, monasteries, town halls and other places. On a road with few hostels, that matters: a church or town hall stamp is as good as any.
Getting there, and back

Madrid is the capital and largest city of Spain. Its airport is ~13 km north-east of the Puerta del Sol, and Wikipedia calls it the country's busiest, with 68.1 million passengers in 2025. The road starts in the old centre, near the Royal Palace, so you can begin on foot from wherever you sleep.

Getting home is the question to settle early. Sahagún is a small town. Look up trains and buses before you go, and do not plan a tight connection for the day you finish. Cercedilla has a railway station on the Madrid–Segovia line, which the Association's guide says it has had since 1888, and the Confraternity says you can take the train from Cercedilla to Segovia if the sierra is closed to you.
Training and pace

The Junta's guide says you do not need to be a highly trained athlete, but you should pace your effort to your possibilities, and train with walking sessions beforehand. It suggests starting with shorter stages, adding longer ones after the first week, and averaging ~25 to ~30 km a day. It also advises an occasional rest day.

For this road, do one thing in particular: walk a ~30 km day at home, with your pack, before you leave. The days over the sierra and across the pine country are of that size, and there are few places to stop partway.
What to carry

Light. The Association's leaflets say no more than ten percent of your body weight, and preferably never more than ~6 to ~7 kg. The Junta's guide says the same rule of a tenth, and warns that over ~8 kg you may regret it.

items.t: Footwear.

The Junta recommends light boots that let your feet breathe and protect your ankles, with trainers as an option in summer. Whatever you choose, it must not be new. The Association's leaflets add petroleum jelly and technical socks against blisters, and the advice to stop at the first sign of rubbing and look at the spot.
Layers and rain gear.
The Confraternity says to expect mountain weather from Madrid to Segovia. Carry a waterproof that also covers your pack, and a warm layer even in summer for the pass.
Sun.
Hat and sun cream. The Junta advises against wearing only a T-shirt and shorts in the first few days.
A sleeping bag,
which the Junta calls essential for pilgrims' hostels. A light one in summer, a warmer one in winter, the Association's leaflets say.
Water and food.
The Junta says to keep your bottle full at all times, and not to carry more than a day's food. On this road, add water for the long gaps (day 4, day 7) and fill up at the last village before them.
A small first-aid kit.
The Junta lists plasters, an anti-inflammatory cream and sun cream, among other things.
Documents.
Your credencial, your identity document, and your health card or European health card if you come from abroad, the Junta says.

spans.t: Money, phones and people at home

The Association's leaflets say there is no need to carry large sums, and that there are cash machines in the main towns. The Junta advises using cards rather than cash. Villages are small, so keep a little cash for them.
Tell someone at home your plan, as the Junta advises, and leave them your list of days. Do not rely on a phone signal everywhere. Save your maps before the sierra.
Language
Spanish is the language of the road. The Confraternity says it is not impossible to walk it without any Spanish, and strongly urges you to learn as much as you can before you set out.
Guides and waymarks

The road is marked with yellow arrows, and the Association says a group of its members goes over the markings every spring. In the city of Madrid itself the Association's guide, in its 2014 edition, says the way is not waymarked: the arrows begin at the Plaza de Castilla, so use a map for the streets before it.

Two guides are worth having, and both can be downloaded from their publishers. The Association's guide has maps at 1:50,000 and a description of every place on the road, in Spanish. The Junta's pilgrim guide, 144 pages in the edition read for this book, is published in Spanish, English, French and German, and has a table of distances from Madrid to Sahagún. Both are named at the end of this book.

chapters.title: Madrid and the Sierra: Madrid to Segovia

spans.t: The character of these days
Four days, ~101 km, from the pavements of a capital to the top of a granite range and down the far side. The first three days follow the foot of the Sierra de Guadarrama and the fourth crosses it.

The distances in this chapter and the next two are the Junta's: each day is the sum of the town-to-town figures in the table of the Junta de Castilla y León's pilgrim guide. The Association's guide, which counts kilometres its own way, comes within ~3 km on most days, and the text says where it differs more. Neither guide divides the road into stages, so the thirteen days of this book are this book's own grouping. The first four match the four stages the Comunidad de Madrid's tourism pages list from Madrid to Segovia. Many pilgrims split the road differently, and the choices chapter shows where.
Day 1: Madrid to Tres Cantos (~23 km)

You start at the church on the Plaza de Santiago and walk north through the old city. The Association's guide counts ~11 km of Madrid's streets before open country, and in its 2014 edition the arrows begin only at the Plaza de Castilla, so carry a map for the first part. The way goes up the Castellana, past four skyscrapers and two hospitals, and through Fuencarral, once a village and now a district.

After that the city thins into a path between the railway and the long wall of the Monte de El Pardo, a Mediterranean forest that the guide says was a royal hunting ground by the fourteenth century. Tres Cantos is a young town: the guide says it was planned in the 1970s and its first residents arrived in 1982. A granite waymarker erected by the Comunidad de Madrid in 2004 stands by the path, and you can have your credencial stamped in the town. About half of today is city, and the rise is gentle. Do not push the pace.
Day 2: Tres Cantos to Manzanares el Real (~28 km)

The Association's guide puts the day at ~27 km. The path climbs along the stream of the Tejada and crosses it on stepping blocks, up to eleven times, and the guide warns that in rainy periods the water can cover the blocks and you must take your shoes off.

Colmenar Viejo, ~12 km from the start, is a natural place to split the day, with ~16 km still to go. Its church, the guide says, has a noble coat of arms carved with scallop shells over the door. Beyond it you follow a
cañada

and cross the Manzanares river by the bridge of the Batán, which the guide calls Roman. Manzanares el Real sits at the foot of La Pedriza, with a fifteenth-century castle. The Camino Mendocino, a road from Guadalajara, joins the Camino de Madrid here, the Comunidad de Madrid says.
Day 3: Manzanares el Real to Cercedilla (~20 km)

The Comunidad de Madrid describes this stage as one at the foot of La Pedriza that takes you fully into the sierra, and the Junta's guide calls the stretch around Mataelpino demanding. The Association's guide has the path leaving Manzanares westward, crossing the Collado de la Jarosa, and reaching Mataelpino at ~1,080 m, below the peak of La Maliciosa.

Then comes Navacerrada, ~1,200 m, a town. It shares its name with the road pass higher up the range, which is not your route: the Association's guide crosses the road that climbs to it and goes on by tracks to Cercedilla. Cercedilla, at the foot of the Siete Picos, was a Roman
mansio

, a staging post, on the same road you will walk tomorrow, and the guide says it has had a station on the Madrid–Segovia line since 1888. Fill your bottles here. Tomorrow, on the direct way, has no village on it.
Day 4: Cercedilla to Segovia (~31 km)

The big day. The Association's guide counts ~31 km between Cercedilla and Segovia, the longest gap between settlements on the whole road. The Confraternity of St James says the climb is ~650 m in ~8 km, on the old Roman road, to the Puerto de la Fuenfría. Sources give the pass at ~1,790 m (the Comunidad de Madrid) and ~1,796 m (the Association and the Junta). At the top runs the boundary between the Comunidad de Madrid and Castilla y León, and a plaque of 2005 remembers the Association's founding president, José Antonio Cimadevila.
The descent is long and easy. The guide mentions the ruins of an old post house and of the inn that Cervantes names in
Rinconete y Cortadillo

; below them you reach the Cruz de la Gallega, a viewpoint over the whole Castilian plain. There you can go straight on to Segovia or detour east by Valsaín to La Granja. The way into Segovia passes the Roman aqueduct, ~28 m high and built without mortar, the Junta's guide says.
Check the weather the day before. The Confraternity says to avoid the sierra in snow or bad weather: there are no farms, villages or facilities. The choices chapter has the alternative.

chapters.title: The Pine Country: Segovia to Puente Duero

spans.t: The character of these days

Four days, ~103 km, across the Tierra de Pinares. The Association's guide describes it as an immense plain, ~100 km long on this road, dotted with pine woods and cut by river gorges, with no mountains, only low plateaus and eroded valleys. It is flat, wide and often quiet.

The pines grow on sand, old dunes that the trees have fixed, the guide says, and the sand is the thing to respect. It slows you down and, the guide warns, can injure you if you try to keep your usual speed. From just before Añe to Simancas it counts more than ten pine woods, adding up to ~30 km in a stretch of ~87 km. Take it slowly, and never force the pace on loose ground.
Day 5: Segovia to Santa María la Real de Nieva (~32 km)

You leave Segovia by the Puerta de Santiago in the old wall, and the Association's guide traces the way: past the site of a vanished Romanesque church of Santiago, down the walk named for Saint John of the Cross, who liked to stroll there, over the Eresma river, then past the Gothic monastery of El Parral and the octagonal Romanesque church of the Vera Cruz, which it dates to the early thirteenth century.

The villages that follow, Zamarramala, Valseca and Los Huertos, are small. Near Los Huertos the path follows an old railway line, the Segovia–Medina del Campo line that ran from 1884 to 1985 and has been a greenway since 2013, the guide says. Past the Eresma the first sandy pine wood begins. Añe is ~21 km from Segovia and a natural place to split the day, with ~11 km left. Santa María la Real de Nieva was founded in 1392, the guide says, by Catherine of Lancaster after a shepherd's vision of the Virgin, and its monastery church holds the grave of Blanche of Navarre, who died there in 1441.
Day 6: Santa María la Real de Nieva to Coca (~19 km)

The Association counts ~22 km, so call it ~19 to ~22. Nieva is only ~2 km on from Santa María, the shortest gap between settlements on the whole road, the Association says, with a Romanesque-Mudéjar church. Then the Tierra de Pinares proper: a sandy plain of pines, with the high-speed railway running alongside for a while. Nava de la Asunción comes ~10 km after Nieva.

The path enters the gorge of the Eresma and follows it through a large pine wood to Coca. The Association's guide says the town was Celtiberian and then Roman, that its walls are Roman in origin and were rebuilt in the Middle Ages, and that it has a fifteenth-century Mudéjar castle. It calls Coca the birthplace of the emperor Theodosius the Great. It is a short day, with time left to see the town.
Day 7: Coca to Alcazarén (~28 km)

Again the sources part: the Association counts ~25 km. You leave Coca by the tower of San Nicolás, cross the river Voltoya, and follow a wide track through pines beside the Eresma to Villeguillo, ~7 to ~10 km on, depending on the guide.

Beyond it the road becomes the Cañada de los Gallegos, also called the Cañada Real de Madrid. Galician reapers walked it, and the Mesta's flocks, and the Association says the three names tell its story:
real
for the stockmen,
de los Gallegos
for the reapers, and
de Madrid

for its reach. After ~2 km you cross from Segovia into Valladolid province. The ~18 km from Villeguillo to Alcazarén are the second longest gap between settlements on the road, the Association says, and the Junta's table gives the same ~18 km. Carry water and food for all of it. Alcazarén is the first town in Valladolid province on the road, and the Junta's guide describes its Romanesque-Mudéjar church of Santiago, with an altarpiece to the Apostle.
Day 8: Alcazarén to Puente Duero (~24 km)

Valdestillas, ~16 km on, has a name that the Junta's guide explains: the "Valle de las Astillas", the valley of the splinters, from the timber that grew here. A bridge over the Adaja there has cutwaters and an arch that the Junta's guide says go back to the Romans.

Then ~8 km more to Puente Duero. Its medieval bridge over the Duero was blown up by the French in 1812 and rebuilt in the middle of the nineteenth century, the Association's guide says, and the village has been part of Valladolid since 1960. Here the road divides: straight on to Simancas, or north-east into the city. The choices chapter explains both. One more pine wood waits on the way to Simancas, the last of the road, the Association says.

chapters.title: The Torozos and Tierra de Campos: Puente Duero to Sahagún

spans.t: The character of these days

Five days, ~122 km, from the Duero to Sahagún across two kinds of high plain. The Association's guide calls the first, the Montes Torozos, a plateau without horizons that gives a false sense of altitude, ~50 km of dry uplands broken by shallow valleys. It calls the second, the Tierra de Campos, an immense steppe with almost no trees except along the rivers, where cereal fields run out until they meet the sky, and where, near the end, the crest of the Cantabrian mountains shows to the north. The Confraternity of St James adds that the villages sit on spurs above steep-sided ravines.
There is little shade here. Carry water, start early in warm weather, and expect long views and long straight tracks.
Day 9: Puente Duero to Peñaflor de Hornija (~27 km)

The Association counts ~26 km. You walk by the river to Simancas, ~6 km on, with its long medieval bridge over the Pisuerga and its castle, which holds the General Archive of Simancas. The Association's guide says the Romans knew it as Septimanca, and that in 939 a Castilian-Leonese army beat that of Abd al-Rahman III here.

Leaving Simancas, the guide says, you go under the motorway by a pedestrian underpass, and the track rises gently over cereal fields to Ciguñuela, whose church has two images of Saint James. Then Wamba, with its Romanesque church. The guide says the Visigothic king Recesvinto died here in 672 and was first buried here, and that his successor, Wamba, was chosen here. Peñaflor de Hornija is ~7 km beyond.
Day 10: Peñaflor de Hornija to Medina de Rioseco (~23 km)

The Association counts ~24 km. Castromonte comes ~9 km on. Off the road, the Junta's guide says, lies the monastery of La Santa Espina, ~6 km from Castromonte, founded in 1147 and named for a relic, a thorn said to come from Christ's crown. It is a side trip, not part of the day.

Medina de Rioseco is a town of churches. The Junta's guide singles out its church of Santiago for its size and its wealth of images of Saint James. The Association adds that the town is where one branch of the Canal de Castilla ends, and that tradition says Saint Francis of Assisi reached it from Sahagún, on his pilgrimage to Compostela, between 1213 and 1215. From here the Tierra de Campos begins.
Day 11: Medina de Rioseco to Cuenca de Campos (~27 km)

Here the guides differ most: the Association counts ~22 km, the Junta ~27 km, and the gap sits in the first half of the day. Take the longer figure for your planning. You pass Berrueces and Tamariz de Campos, then Moral de la Reina, ~19 km from Medina on the Junta's table (the Association says ~14 km) and ~8 km short of Cuenca de Campos, which makes a natural place to split the day. The Association's guide says Moral de la Reina has two small bridges of Roman origin.

One warning from the Association: near the boundary between Medina de Rioseco and Berrueces the path runs for a few hundred metres on the verge of the N-601, a national road. Face the traffic, keep to the edge, and cross only where you can see.
Day 12: Cuenca de Campos to Santervás de Campos (~22 km)

Both guides agree on ~22 km. After ~5 km comes Villalón de Campos. Then Fontihoyuelo, where, the Association says, the wooden columns of the humble church's porch are carved with scallop shells and pilgrim staffs. Santervás de Campos follows, ~10 km on, with a Romanesque-Mudéjar church of the twelfth century on the river Valderaduey.
The Association notes that the road leaves the province of Valladolid and enters León just beyond. Tomorrow is the last day before the join. The land has risen a little, and it is still open.
Day 13: Santervás de Campos to Sahagún (~23 km)

Melgar de Arriba and Arenillas de Valderaduey come first, then Grajal de Campos with its castle, begun in 1517 and one of the last in Spain built to withstand the artillery of its time, the Association says. Beyond Grajal the Association gives two ways: by San Pedro de las Dueñas, with its Gothic-Mudéjar monastery, or straight to Sahagún.

Just before the town stands the sanctuary of the Virgen Peregrina, a former Franciscan convent restored in 2011. The Association says the carved Virgin there, dressed as a pilgrim with a staff, dates from 1687 and has been patron of the Camino de Madrid since 2013.

Sahagún lies between the rivers Cea and Valderaduey. The Junta's guide calls it a major milestone on the Pilgrims' Route, the end of the seventh stage of the Codex Calixtinus. The Association's guide counts ~355 km from here to Santiago, and the Junta ~364 km. You leave by crossing the Cea on the Puente de Cantos, and from there you are on the Camino Francés.
How many days?

The sources do not agree. The Confraternity of St James says about two weeks without rest days. The Comunidad de Madrid's tourism pages say the road is completed in ten stages to Sahagún, four of them from Madrid to Segovia, which means days of ~32 km on average, by simple division. The Junta's guide recommends an average of ~25 to ~30 km. This book uses thirteen, between towns about a day apart. Neither printed guide divides the road into stages, so no division is official, and many pilgrims cut it differently.
Halfway points on the long days

These are places on the road, not promises of a bed. A split is only useful if you can sleep at the end of it, so ask the app and the Association's hostel notes before you decide. Distances come from the Junta's table. The Association's figures agree within a kilometre or two, except for Moral de la Reina, which it puts ~14 km from Medina de Rioseco.

items.t: Day 2, Tres Cantos to Manzanares el Real:
Colmenar Viejo, ~12 km from the start and ~16 km before the end.
Day 4, Cercedilla to Segovia:

on the direct way there is no village. The detour east from the Cruz de la Gallega to Valsaín and La Granja, which the Junta's table follows, puts La Granja ~18 km from Cercedilla and ~13 km from Segovia.
Day 5, Segovia to Santa María la Real de Nieva:
Añe, ~21 km from Segovia and ~11 km from the end.
Day 8, Alcazarén to Puente Duero:
Valdestillas, ~16 km and ~8 km.
Day 11, Medina de Rioseco to Cuenca de Campos:
Moral de la Reina, ~19 km and ~8 km on the Junta's table.

spans.t: If the sierra is closed to you

The Association's guide says that when it snows the Puerto de la Fuenfría can be impassable. In that case it advises using the road and crossing the range by the nearby Navacerrada pass, which, it says, has snowploughs all year. That is a road, with traffic, not a path. The Confraternity says you can instead take the train from Cercedilla to Segovia. Decide in Cercedilla, with the forecast and the local news, not on the pass. The Confraternity's rule is simple: avoid the sierra in snow or bad weather.
Simancas or Valladolid

At Puente Duero the Junta's guide gives two ways. The main one goes ~6 km to Simancas. The other goes ~12 km into Valladolid, the regional capital, then ~14 km from the city to Simancas, by a local road or by tracks. That makes the Valladolid way ~20 km longer. The Association's guide also offers a track from the city straight to Ciguñuela, with a steep climb at the start.
Valladolid is the seat of the regional government, since 1983 according to the Association's guide, and its cathedral dates from the late sixteenth century, the Junta says.
Side trips and joining roads

items.t: La Santa Espina
, the monastery founded in 1147, is ~6 km from Castromonte on day 10, the Junta's guide says.
The Camino Mendocino
begins in the province of Guadalajara and joins the Camino de Madrid at Manzanares el Real, the Comunidad de Madrid says. From there its walkers share the road with you.
Sahagún and beyond.
The Camino de Madrid ends where it meets the Camino Francés. You may go home from Sahagún, or walk on.
The French Way
in this series covers the road from there.

spans.t: Where you sleep
An
albergue
is a pilgrims' hostel: shared rooms and bunk beds. The Association's guide says hospitality on this road is offered by parishes, town councils, institutions and private people. Some work on a
donativo
basis, which means you give what you can. The Association's leaflets are firm that
donativo
does not mean the stay costs nothing: give at least what it has cost the hosts.

Plan for fewer beds than on the busy roads. The app's route notes say lodging is sparse and tell you to check municipal hostels. The Association's guide counts ~14 km as the average distance between places that host pilgrims, with the sierra gap of ~31 km. The Confraternity of St James says there is more accommodation than you might expect for so few towns, but that guesthouses and small hotels come at intervals of ~30 km, and that between Simancas and Sahagún only two places offer them on the road itself. It also says that donation-based and inexpensive pilgrim hostels are limited, and campsites very few.
This book names no hostel, and does not say which towns have one, because that changes. Three ways to find out:

items.t: Look in the CaminoPlus app.
Look at the Association's news page. It has published dated notes on the state of the road's hostels, the latest seen for this book being from 1 October 2026.
Ask as you go. The Association's leaflets say to confirm in each hostel which ones are open for the next stretch, in winter and even in summer.

spans.t: Advice on booking differs. The Junta's guide says the pilgrim hostels take no reservations, and that large groups should look for other places to sleep. The Association's leaflets say to book a bed if in doubt. Both can be true, since hostels differ. If a stage is long and the next bed is far, a call ahead is worth making.
Hostel manners
The leaflets set out a few rules that apply on any Camino, and they matter more where beds are few.

items.t: Respect the
hospitaleros
, the volunteers or staff who host you, and the other pilgrims.
Lights go out in the late evening and rooms must be empty again early in the morning.
Keep your pack on the floor, never on a bunk, since it can carry unwelcome insects in from the road.
Carry a sleeping bag, which the Junta calls essential.

spans.t: What you eat

You will often be far from a shop. The Association's leaflets say there are shops in the main towns, and that you should carry little food. On this road that means: carry enough for the long days (the sierra, and the ~18 km before Alcazarén), and buy what you can in the last village before them. The Junta's guide says not to carry more than a day's food and to keep your water bottle full. The Association adds that heavy meals before you arrive are best avoided.
In the evening you will find what each place offers. You may be offered a
menú del peregrino
, a set meal for pilgrims, but ask. The Junta's guide says Segovia's hallmark dish is roast suckling pig. Beyond that, eat what the village eats.
Rest days
The Junta's guide suggests an occasional rest day, or alternating longer days with shorter ones that end in places where you would like to stay longer. On this road the choice of place is easy.
Segovia

is the natural one, after the sierra. Its aqueduct and old town are on the UNESCO World Heritage list, which the Association's guide dates to 1985, and the Junta's guide calls its cathedral the last Gothic cathedral built in Spain. The Confraternity says that even Segovia is a collection of small village centres, which may suit you after the pass.
Coca
and
Medina de Rioseco
are smaller and quieter, with castle and churches, if you would rather rest in a town of a few thousand people than in a city.
If you would rather rest in a big city, the detour to Valladolid is one of the choices described in the chapter before this one.
This chapter is plain on purpose. On a quiet road you are your own first help, so read it before the first day, and again before the pass.
The sierra

The climb to the Puerto de la Fuenfría is ~650 m in ~8 km, on a Roman road, and the day is ~31 km long. The Confraternity of St James says the sierra has mountain weather, that snow can lie there until May, and that there are no farms, villages or facilities on it. Its advice is to avoid the sierra in snow or bad weather. The Association's guide adds that fog is a hazard, here and on the plains, and that the pass can be impassable in snow.

items.t: Decide in Cercedilla, not on the pass. Look at the forecast and at the sky.
Start early, so the crossing is in daylight with time in hand.
Carry water, food, a waterproof and a warm layer, even in summer.
Know the alternatives (the choices chapter): the road over the Navacerrada pass, or the train from Cercedilla to Segovia.
The stretch from the upper Fuenfría valley to the edge of Segovia lies inside the Sierra de Guadarrama National Park, the Association's guide says, so follow the park's rules, and light no fire.

spans.t: The descent is long and gentle, but it is long. Walk it slowly, for your knees.
Heat and sun
The Confraternity says July to early September is extremely hot, with long stretches of the road having absolutely no shade. That is the main danger of this road, more than the hills.

items.t: Start at first light and aim to finish before the afternoon.
Carry more water than you think you need, and fill up at the last village before a long gap: the sierra, and the ~18 km before Alcazarén.
Wear a hat and sun cream. The Junta's guide advises against walking in only a T-shirt and shorts at the start.
Do not plan your longest days for the hottest week. Split them, or rest.
If you feel dizzy, sick or confused, stop in shade, drink, and ask for help. If it does not pass, call 112, the European emergency number.

spans.t: Cold, rain and fog

In winter the Association's guide says fog can be intense and persistent in the sierra and in Castile, and that you should carry a means of orientation, or use the nearest road, with the usual care. A waterproof that covers your pack, the leaflets say, is part of the basic kit. Daylight is short, about 9 hours at midwinter, so a long day needs an early start.
Sand

In the pine woods the sandy ground slows you. The Association's guide warns that forcing the pace on it risks injury, whether you walk, cycle or ride. Shorten your stride, let the pace fall, and plan fewer kilometres on the days with the most woodland.
Roads and streams

Only a small part of the way is on tarmac, but it is not nothing: the Association counts ~42 km of town streets, ~11 km of them in Madrid. The Junta's guide reminds you that on roads you are the most vulnerable, and that drivers may not see a person on foot.

items.t: Walk facing the traffic, keep to the edge, and wear something bright.
Near the boundary between Medina de Rioseco and Berrueces the Association's guide has a few hundred metres on the verge of the N-601. Take care there.
On day 2 the path crosses the Tejada stream on stepping blocks. In rain the water can cover them, and the guide says to take your shoes off to cross.

spans.t: Fire
The Confraternity says wild camping in the pine woods is not recommended, because of the risk of fire. Treat that as a rule: do not light a fire, and do not smoke where the ground is dry.
On your own
Very few pilgrims walk this road, so you may be alone for hours.

items.t: Tell someone at home your plan, as the Junta's guide advises, and send a message each evening.
Charge your phone, save your maps, and do not count on a signal everywhere.
Look after your feet. The Association's leaflets advise petroleum jelly and technical socks, and stopping at the first rubbing to look at it.
Stop when you need to. A short day is never a failure, and a rest day is part of the plan.
See a doctor about anything that worries you, before you leave and on the road. Carry your health card, or your European health card if you come from abroad.

spans.t: People walk for many reasons: faith, sport, grief, curiosity, a rest from work, a promise, a milestone birthday. None of them is the wrong one, and you do not have to explain yours to anyone on the road.
A road of solitude
This road asks something different from a crowded Camino. The Confraternity of St James says it appeals to people who want solitude and the wide horizons of the
meseta
. Very few pilgrims walk it, so the company you keep is mostly your own, the sky, and the people of the villages you pass.
That can be a gift or a weight. Some days the plain will feel like room to think, and some days like a long empty hour. Both are normal, and both pass.
Leaving from home

Most Caminos begin with a journey: a plane, a train, a first night in a strange town. This one can begin at your own front door. The Association's guide says the road was recovered so that a pilgrim from Madrid could set out for Compostela from the
puerta de casa
, the door of home. If you live in Madrid, you may find that leaving the place you know best asks more of you than leaving one you do not know at all.
Those who walked it before

Shepherds and harvesters used this road long before pilgrims did. For almost five hundred years, until the railway came, Galician reapers walked these tracks to cut the grain of Castile, and the Association's guide calls them the nearest ancestors of today's pilgrims here. They were not looking for a certificate. They walked for work, a long way from home.
You may find it a good company to keep when the path is hard. People crossed this plain on foot for much plainer reasons than yours, season after season.
The Association says it marked the road in a pilgrim spirit and not as a hiker's route, and adds that nobody minds if you begin as a walker. You may end as something else, or you may not.
Questions for the walk
Choose one a day. Do not answer it before lunch.

items.t: What are you carrying that you could leave behind?
What does the empty plain ask you to stop doing?
Who would you like to walk this stretch with, and what would you say to them?
What are you walking towards, and what are you walking away from?
What do you notice when no one is watching?
When did you last do something slowly, and what happened?

spans.t: One small practice

On a day of long straight track, walk an hour without your phone or music. Notice what you hear: your own feet, wind in the crops, a tractor far off. At the end of the day, write down three lines about it. They do not have to be good.
The end of this road

This road ends in Sahagún, not in Santiago. You arrive on the thirteenth day, past the sanctuary of the Virgen Peregrina, into a small town of about 2,400 inhabitants, Wikipedia says, between two rivers. The Association's guide says that it grew around a monastery of the martyrs Facundus and Primitivus, of which little remains. The Junta's guide calls Sahagún a major milestone on the Pilgrims' Route, the end of the seventh stage in the Codex Calixtinus. Wikipedia says it holds some of the earliest examples of Mudéjar architecture, a Spanish style that joins Islamic decoration to Christian buildings.

You leave it, the Association's guide says, over the Puente de Cantos on the river Cea. That is where the Camino de Madrid becomes the Camino Francés. From there Santiago is ~355 km on the Association's count and ~364 km on the Junta's, which is ~12 to ~15 days at the Junta's pace.
The French Way
, in this series, takes the road from here.
The Compostela

The Compostela is the certificate the Pilgrim's Office in Santiago gives to those who meet its rules. The Office owns the rules, and they can change. This book says what the Office says, and sends you to the Office in any doubt.

items.t: The Compostela is for those who come to the tomb of the Apostle for religious and/or spiritual reasons and follow the routes of the Way of St James on foot, by bicycle or on horseback.
It asks for at least the last hundred kilometres on foot or on horseback, or the last two hundred kilometres by bicycle, shown by the credencial, stamped along the route.

On foot or on horseback, that means at least a hundred continuous kilometres on the same route to Santiago that the Office recognises. The final stage must include at least the last one leading into the cathedral.

You may walk the Way in stages, if they follow in chronological and geographical order. A pilgrim who walks only the minimum distance must get the credencial stamped at the start and at the end of each stage, with the date.
A pilgrim who has already walked part of a recognised route outside Spain needs no less than seventy kilometres in Spain.
The Cabildo, the cathedral's governing council, reserves the right to grant the Compostela in special and exceptional cases.

spans.t: The Office awards the Compostela to those who walk for religious or spiritual reasons, and it describes the pilgrimage it has in mind as one made "with a Christian sentiment, even if it is only with an attitude of search". If that does not describe your reason for walking, ask the Pilgrim's Office what it can give you: it also offers a Certificate of Distance, which records the kilometres you walked from wherever you started.
What this means from Madrid

From Madrid you have ~320 km to Sahagún and then ~355 to ~365 km to Santiago, so ~675 to ~690 km in all. That is far more than the last hundred kilometres the Office asks for. Those last hundred kilometres lie on the Camino Francés, beyond Sahagún, and
The French Way
covers them.

The Office issues the Compostela in Santiago, and its rule asks for the final stage to include the last steps into the cathedral. If you walk only the Camino de Madrid, you finish in Sahagún, short of it. The Office's pages on the Compostela, the credencial and the Certificate of Distance, read for this book, speak of "any of the routes recognized by the International Pilgrim's Reception Office system", and they do not name the Camino de Madrid. If you plan to walk in stages, or you want to know how the Office treats a walk that began in Madrid, ask the Pilgrim's Office before you go. This book does not say whether any other start counts.
Keep your credencial from Madrid with you the whole way, and have it stamped as you go. The Office asks for it stamped along the route.
At the Pilgrim's Office

The Office issues the Compostela, a document in Latin. Procedures and hours change, so look at the Office's own website before you arrive in Santiago, and do not plan a tight connection for the same day.
Whatever the Compostela means to you, it is a record of a road you walked, not a measure of it.
Your day in Sahagún
Do not leave on the morning after you arrive.

items.t: Rest.
You have walked ~325 km on the Junta's figures.
Look around.
The Association's guide names the arch of San Benito and the chapel of San Mando, both remains of the old monastery, and several Mudéjar churches.
Decide.
If you walk on, the next day is the Camino Francés. If you go home, plan your way with the timetables in front of you.

spans.t: If you walked on from Sahagún,
The French Way

has taken you the rest of the way, and this chapter belongs to a later day. If you stopped in Sahagún, you have walked ~325 km on the Junta's figures, and that is a Camino whatever the paperwork says.
The first week back

Expect the quiet to feel odd. After days when the only schedule was your own legs, a calendar full of meetings can feel loud. Give yourself a slow first day, if you can. Sleep. Unpack your pack on the floor, as the hostels taught you.
Look at your credencial. The stamps from Madrid, Segovia and the small villages in between are a map of where you were, and many walkers keep them for years.
Keeping the road alive

items.t: Write it down
while the days are still sharp: the long gaps, the pass, the plain. A few lines each evening and a longer note on your first day at home.
Stay in touch
with the people you met, in the hostels or on the way.
Join a local association.

The Madrid association says it organises a weekend walk on the Caminos of Spain, Portugal and France in most months from September to June, and that many of its members serve as volunteer hosts in hostels that run on donations. Its website has the details, and other cities have associations of their own.
Walk again.
Sahagún is a good place to have stopped, because the next day is waiting there: the Camino Francés carries on towards Santiago whenever you are ready.

spans.t: The road will still be there. The Association says its volunteers go over the yellow arrows every spring.
With the CaminoPlus app
CaminoPlus
is the offline-first companion app for the Camino de Santiago, with maps that work without signal, stays and cafes, a pilgrim passport with stamps, a journal and friends. The paid plan is called
Pilgrim Plus

. The app is still in development. The Camino de Madrid is on its list of routes, from Madrid to Sahagún, but this book makes no claim about what the app holds for it today, so look in the app, and use it, not this book, for beds, cafes, closures and weather.

A reminder about the passport: the Pilgrim's Office asks for the stamped credencial. A passport in CaminoPlus, or in any app other than the Office's own digital credential, is a keepsake until the Office says otherwise.
Sources and thanks
This book rests on public sources, and its fact ledger lists every fact against the page it came from. The chief ones are:

items.t: The Junta de Castilla y León
(turismocastillayleon.com): its tourism pages on the Camino de Santiago de Madrid and on the Madrid cycling route, read in Spanish, and its pilgrim guide
The Madrid Route: A Practical Guide for Pilgrims
(Spanish original
Guía del Peregrino del Camino de Madrid
), published by the Fundación Siglo para el Turismo y las Artes de Castilla y León, read in the English edition of June 2020.
The Asociación de Amigos de los Caminos de Santiago de Madrid
(demadridalcamino.com): its guide
Camino de Madrid a Santiago de Compostela: Cartografía e itinerario Madrid-Sahagún
(first edition, July 2014, in Spanish), its pages on the credencial and on who it is, its seasonal leaflets of 2021, and the title and date of its hostel-status notice of 1 October 2026.
The Comunidad de Madrid
, on its tourism site (visitmadrid.es): the page on the Camino de Santiago in the Comunidad, in Spanish.
The Confraternity of St James
(csj.org.uk): its page on the Camino de Madrid, published in 2020 and updated in 2025.
The Pilgrim's Reception Office of the Cathedral of Santiago
(oficinadelperegrino.com): its pages on the Compostela, the credencial and the Certificate of Distance.
Wikipedia
, for climate tables (Valladolid, Segovia, Madrid), for the articles on Sahagún, Madrid and Madrid's airport, and for the infobox of the Spanish article on the Camino de Santiago de Madrid.
A standard solar calculation
, for the hours of daylight.
The CaminoPlus route catalog and route notes
, for the route's start, end, ~320 km, difficulty rating and best months.

spans.t: Published figures differ between these sources, so every distance in this book is marked ~. Where the sources say nothing, for example on closing dates, the book says nothing and tells you to check. If you know a better figure, or a fact that has changed, tell CaminoPlus.
Thanks go to the people who keep the Way: the volunteers who paint the yellow arrows each spring, the hosts who open the hostels, and the people of the villages who point the way and say
Buen Camino
to a stranger.
A short glossary

items.t: Albergue
: a pilgrims' hostel with shared rooms.
Buen Camino
: "good Way", the greeting between pilgrims.
Cabildo
: the governing council of the cathedral.
Cañada
: a historic drove road for livestock.
Compostela
: the Latin certificate the Pilgrim's Office issues.
Credencial
: the pilgrim's passport.
Donativo
: a hostel that asks a donation instead of a fixed charge.
Hospitalero
: the host of a pilgrims' hostel.
Menú del peregrino
: a set meal for pilgrims.
Meseta
: the high plain of central Spain.
Mudéjar
: a Spanish style that joins Islamic decoration to Christian buildings.
Puerto
: a mountain pass.
Sello
: a stamp in the credencial.
